parsed.summary: The theorem says: for every a.e.-strongly-measurable f : ℝ/2πℤ → ℂ with ∫ |f| log(2+|f|) dμ < ∞, where μ is normalized Haar measure, there is a measurable null set E off which the symmetric Fourier partial sums S_N f(x) = Σ_{|k|≤N} f̂(k) e^{ikx} converge to f(x) as N → ∞ along all N. This matches Theorem 1.1 faithfully. The integrability hypothesis implies f ∈ L¹, so `fourierCoeff` is not a junk value. No significant caveat was found; only the auxiliary weak-L¹ maximal corollary is left unformalized.

glossary.plain: Instance recording 0 < 2π, needed to use AddCircle (2π) and its Haar probability measure.
Normalized (probability) Haar measure on T = ℝ/2πℤ, i.e. dx/2π.
glossary.standard_concept: normalized Lebesgue measure μ on T
glossary.note: Null sets agree with those of Lebesgue measure, and the normalization matches the standard Fourier coefficient convention.
Would be junk 0 if the integrand were not integrable, but f ∈ L¹ follows from the hypothesis.

lean_claims.plain: For all f : ℝ/2πℤ → ℂ that are a.e.-strongly measurable with x ↦ |f(x)| log(2+|f(x)|) integrable for normalized Haar measure μ, there exists a measurable E with μ(E) = 0 such that for every x ∉ E, Σ_{k=-N}^{N} f̂(k) e^{ikx} → f(x) as N → ∞ (N ∈ ℕ).

paper_claims.plain: For every complex-valued f ∈ L log L(T), i.e. ∫ |f| log(2+|f|) dμ < ∞, there is a measurable null set N_f with lim_{N→∞} S_N f(x) = f(x) for x ∈ T \ N_f, along the full sequence N = 0, 1, 2, …
Luxemburg-norm weak-L¹ maximal bound for the partial sums (via Stein's theorem); details not in excerpt.

coverage.why: Same class (|f| log(2+|f|) integrable), same symmetric partial sums, full-sequence limit, measurable null exceptional set.
The maximal weak-L¹ bound is not stated in Lean.

flags.explanation: Only the a.e. convergence theorem is formalized. The weak-L¹ maximal estimate and the intermediate good-set estimate (1.1) are not formalized.

lint_verdicts.why: The argument 2 + ‖f x‖ is always ≥ 2 > 0, so Real.log takes its genuine value; since log(2+t) ≥ log 2 > 0, integrability also implies f ∈ L¹, so fourierCoeff is not junk.
